Development of Respiratory System  
Paul Ganguly
Professor, Alfaisal University

Development of Lungs
l The following power point is intended to 
strengthen my resource (lecture) in the 
class. Please make sure that you have the 
concept before opening the text book.

Molecular studies
l Note that physical stimulus of amniotic fluid plays a 
major role of lung growth. Oligohydramnios will seriously 
affect the growth of lungs. At birth the lungs are half 
filled with fluid derived from the amniotic cavity
l Fetal breathing movements (FBMs) also seem to play a 
role in lung growth through their effects on lung cell 
cycle kinetics by regulating the expression of growth 
factors such as platelet-derived growth factors and 
insulin like growth factors and establishing the gradient 
of thyroid transcription factors expression

The respiratory system
l The respiratory organs (larynx, trachea, 
bronchi and lungs) begin to form during 
the fourth week of development.
l Identify the laryngotracheal diverticulum. 
Remember the endoderm-responsible for 
epithelia of both respiratory and GI 
systems

Observe: 1. Endoderm is becoming tube 2: 
Surroundings of endoderm are coming from 
splanchnic mesoderm

Yellow color-Endoderm; Redish brown color-
Mesoderm for cartilage and muscle

l Respiratory bud starts at the 
laryngotracheal diverticulum (4th week)
l Now think about connection between 
trachea and esophagus
l Why does it need a connection?

The Tracheoesophageal Ridge Forms a Septum to Separate the Trachea
                                                 and Esophagus
I-VI = Pharyngeal arches

Branching and Lobe Formation in the Lungs
Trachea
Visceral pleura

Lung Bud-Endoderm (yellow); Pleura 
(Pink-lateral mesoderm)

Differentiation of Alveolar Cells
16-26 Weeks  
Type I alveolar cells = gas exchange
Type II alveolar cells (6.5-7 months) = surfactant = decreased 
surface tension
16% of alveolar cells are present at birth; remainder develop for 
10 years
Premature infants (<7 months) = respiratory distress syndrome 
(RDS) = insufficient surfactant = increased surface tension = 
collapse of alveoli
32 Weeks

l Follow the development of yolk sac, 
endoderm and intra-embryonic coelom

IEC=Intraembryonic coelom
IEC

Follow the structures during folding of the 
embryo
IEC

Observe-esophagus and two lung buds 
(thorax)-yellow color
Developments of pleura and pericardium

The lungs and heart are covered with 
parietal (somatic) and visceral layer 
(autonomic)

Growing lung covered with two layers; 
pleural cavity is present inside

Matured lung-covered with parietal (phrenic and 
intercostal nerves)  and visceral layers (autonomic)

Lung Development
l Pseudoglandular stage (6 to 16 weeks)
l Canalicular stage (16 to 26 weeks)
l Terminal sac stage (26 weeks to birth)-
important stage for viability of the fetus 
because of adequate surfactant production
l Alveolar stage (32 weeks to 8 years)

Clinical Embryology
l Oligohydramnios and lung development
 (note that fluid in the lung in embryonic 
life is an important stimulus for lung 
development. In oligohydramnios such as 
congenital kidney disease, lung 
development is retarded)
l Agenesis of lungs is possible in congenital 
diaphragmatic hernia where intestinal 
organs come to thorax

l Tracheoesophageal (TO) fistula-is possible 
as the origin is from TO diverticulum
l Respiratory distress syndrome-due to 
defect in surfactant-Type II alveolar cell 
defect
l Pleuropericardial membrane defect-results 
in a communication between pericardial 
and pleural spaces

Tracheoesophageal Fistulas and Atresias 
Caused by Abnormal Septation

Medicolegal case
l Lungs of a stillborn infant are firm and 
sink in water because they contain fluid 
and not air 
Viability of a fetus
l Since lung is almost complete after 28 
weeks, a fetus may survive in the event of 
a premature labor
Development of Diaphragm

Gross anatomy of diaphragm (dome shaped-where 
the upper limit is at T8 and lower limit at T12)
Transverse section of diaphragm

Understanding Myotome-observe the bulbs of this orchid-initially they 
were way up-taking the connecting stalks along with it (similar to 
somatic nerve)!! Think about diaphragm development with C3, 4 and 5 
(previous resource)

Development of Diaphragm-remember these 
four sources

Transverse section at the junction of 
thorax and abdomen

Observe three structures-inferior vena cava, esophagus and 
aorta. Observe also that there is no diaphragm at this 
stage-a thorough passage-Week 4

Three structures are protected by mesentery 
of esophagus (future crus of diaphragm)

Observe the Septum Transversum or Central Tendon 
(supplied by Phrenic Nerve)-thorax and abdomen are 
getting separated

Observe the appearance of pleuroperitoneal 
membrane to close the gap (unstable)

Observe the appearance of lateral body wall 
muscle replacing the membrane (supplied by 
intercostal nerve)

Observe the following diagrams (from your 
text book)
Note the pleuroperitoneal fold
(how it is closing the canal)

Note how the muscle from bodywall is 
growing and slowly replacing the 
pleuroperitoneal membrane

Q. How do the crura of diaphragm 
develop?
 Ans: From the dorsal mesentry of 
esophagus

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
(A posterolateral defect of the diaphragm 
through hernias occur is the most 
common anomaly. The hernia is 
associated with the presence of abdominal 
organs in thorax. Please note that the 
hernia results from defective fusion of the 
pleuroperitoneal membrane with the other 
three parts of the diaphragm)
